lessons.title: Respiration and Cellular Energy
lessons.description: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration, how cells release energy, and why we need it.
lessons.content_html:
Why Every Cell Needs Energy

In the final metres of a 400-metre race, a runner’s muscles begin to burn. Oxygen can no longer be delivered fast enough to sustain the pace, and a different energy pathway kicks in — one that works without oxygen but produces a painful build-up of lactic acid. This is cellular respiration at its limits. But respiration is not just for athletes: it happens continuously in every cell of every living organism, from bacteria to blue whales, twenty-four hours a day.

The energy transferred by respiration powers all life processes: muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, active transport across membranes, protein synthesis and cell division. This energy is stored in a molecule called ATP, which acts as the cell’s immediate energy currency. Respiration is exothermic — it releases energy to the surroundings, which is why your body stays warm even on a cold day.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is NOT breathing. Respiration is an exothermic chemical reaction inside every living cell that transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Breathing (ventilation) is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and takes place in the mitochondria. It completely breaks down glucose and produces a large yield of ATP, making it the most efficient form of respiration. The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\)

Because glucose is completely broken down, aerobic respiration extracts the maximum possible ATP from each glucose molecule. This is why cells with high energy demands — such as muscle cells, liver cells and sperm cells — contain large numbers of mitochondria. The folded inner membranes of the mitochondria (cristae) increase the surface area available for respiration reactions.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient — for example, during intense exercise, or in waterlogged soil. Unlike aerobic respiration, it takes place in the cytoplasm and produces far less ATP because glucose is only partially broken down. The products depend on the type of organism.

In animal cells (and some bacteria), glucose is partially broken down to produce lactic acid:
\(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

Lactic acid builds up in muscles during intense exercise, lowering pH and interfering with enzyme function — causing the burning sensation and fatigue athletes experience. After exercise stops, you continue to breathe deeply to supply the extra oxygen needed to convert accumulated lactic acid back to glucose (in the liver). This extra oxygen requirement is called the oxygen debt (or excess post-exercise oxygen consumption).

In yeast and plant cells, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide:
\(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

This process is called fermentation. It has important commercial applications. In brewing and wine-making, yeast ferments sugar in fruit juice or malt to produce ethanol. In bread-making, yeast ferments sugars in dough, and the CO\(_2\) produced forms bubbles that make the bread rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen, mitochondria): high ATP yield, products are CO\(_2\) + water. Anaerobic in animals (no oxygen, cytoplasm): low ATP, product is lactic acid. Anaerobic in yeast/plants: low ATP, products are ethanol + CO\(_2\).

Respiration During and After Exercise

During exercise, muscle cells need more energy so the rate of respiration increases. The body responds by increasing heart rate (to pump more oxygenated blood to muscles), increasing breathing rate and depth (to take in more O\(_2\) and remove more CO\(_2\)), and breaking down glycogen stores in muscles and the liver into glucose. If exercise is intense enough that oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. The oxygen debt is repaid after exercise as lactic acid is oxidised to CO\(_2\) and water in the liver.

You can detect the products of respiration experimentally. Breathing out through limewater turns it milky, confirming CO\(_2\) production. Placing a temperature probe in a sealed flask with germinating seeds shows a temperature increase over time, confirming that respiration is exothermic. The rate can be measured by monitoring CO\(_2\) output using a carbon dioxide sensor or pH indicator solution.

When interpreting data from these experiments, consider: whether the change observed could have another cause (a confounding variable), whether the results are repeatable, and whether a control is needed (e.g. dead seeds in a sealed flask) to confirm that any heat or gas is coming from the biological process and not a chemical contaminant.

Key Fact

The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration. It is repaid by continued heavy breathing after exercise stops. Lactic acid is converted back to glucose in the liver.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common mistake is confusing respiration with breathing — make this distinction explicit in every answer. When comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration, always state the location (mitochondria vs cytoplasm), the oxygen requirement and the ATP yield. For ‘explain’ questions about exercise responses (increased heart rate, breathing rate), use causal language: explain why each response helps (e.g. ‘increased breathing rate delivers more oxygen to muscles, allowing more aerobic respiration and greater ATP production’). Examiners expect this chain of reasoning, not just a list of changes.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cellular respiration is an exothermic process in all living cells that transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Aerobic respiration (in mitochondria, with oxygen) produces a large ATP yield. Equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\).
  • Anaerobic respiration (in the cytoplasm, without oxygen) produces less ATP. In animals, it produces lactic acid; in yeast and plants, it produces ethanol and CO\(_2\) (fermentation).
  • During intense exercise, lactic acid builds up (oxygen debt). After exercise, continued breathing supplies the extra oxygen needed to convert lactic acid back to glucose in the liver.

practice_questions.text: Compare the products of anaerobic respiration in a human muscle cell and in a yeast cell.

practice_questions.text: A student measures the temperature inside two sealed flasks over 30 minutes. Flask A contains germinating pea seeds; Flask B contains the same mass of boiled (dead) pea seeds. Suggest why the student includes Flask B in the investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Flask B is a control. It shows any temperature change that occurs without biological respiration (e.g. from chemical processes in dead cells or heat from the environment). Comparing Flask A with Flask B allows the student to confirm that any additional temperature rise in Flask A is due to respiration by the living seeds, not to another variable. Without the control, any conclusion about respiration would be unreliable.
Secure: Flask B is a control to show what happens without living seeds, so any difference in Flask A can be attributed to respiration.
Developing: It is a control so you can compare.
Emerging: It is the control.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of fermentation by yeast in two commercial industries. For each, explain both the benefit of the fermentation process and any limitation or risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In bread-making, yeast ferments sugars to produce CO₂, which makes dough rise creating a light texture — the ethanol produced evaporates during baking. A limitation is temperature control: too cold and yeast respires too slowly; too hot and the yeast is killed. In brewing, yeast ferments sugars in grain or fruit juice to produce ethanol for alcoholic drinks. A limitation is that if ethanol concentration rises too high, it becomes toxic to the yeast, halting fermentation. Both industries exploit anaerobic respiration but need careful management of conditions.
Secure: Two industries described with a correct fermentation product for each; one benefit and one limitation per industry.
Developing: Two industries described with products; limited evaluation.
Emerging: One industry described correctly.

lessons.title: Cell Structure and How We Know It
lessons.description: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, organelles, and how microscopy revealed the inside of the cell.
lessons.content_html:
How We Came to Know the Cell

In 1665, Robert Hooke placed a thin slice of cork under a simple microscope and saw a pattern of tiny compartments. He called them “cells” because they reminded him of the small rooms in a monastery. Hooke could not see inside these compartments — his instrument was far too weak. Yet that single observation launched two centuries of investigation, ultimately revealing that cells are the fundamental unit of all life. The history of our understanding of cell structure is a story of technology driving science: each new generation of microscopes unlocked a new layer of biological reality.

This lesson explores two fundamental cell types — eukaryotic and prokaryotic — and traces how improvements in microscopy revealed the internal structures we now know so well.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi) have a true nucleus that encloses DNA within a nuclear membrane. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes are typically 10–100 times smaller than eukaryotes.

Organelles and Their Functions

Both animal and plant cells contain a core set of organelles whose design is closely matched to their function. The exam requires you to go beyond naming structures — you must explain why each structure’s shape, position or composition allows it to carry out its role efficiently.

Nucleus — contains the chromosomes (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The nuclear membrane keeps the genetic material separate from the cytoplasm. When a cell needs a particular protein, the genetic instructions are copied from DNA and sent out through pores in the nuclear membrane to the ribosomes.

Cell membrane — a thin, selectively permeable layer that controls which substances enter and leave. It contains receptor molecules that allow the cell to detect and respond to hormones and other chemical signals.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration. Their folded inner membranes (cristae) greatly increase the surface area available for respiration enzymes, making energy transfer more efficient. Cells with very high energy demands — such as muscle cells or sperm cells — are packed with mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures found in both the cytoplasm and on the endoplasmic reticulum. They are the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes are present in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, though prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller.

Plant cells have all the animal cell structures listed above, plus three additional ones:

Cell wall — made of cellulose, it surrounds the cell membrane and provides structural strength. It is fully permeable (allows all dissolved substances through) but prevents the cell from bursting when water enters by osmosis, keeping the cell turgid and supporting the plant.

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They are found mainly in cells near the surface of leaves and stems where light is available.

Permanent vacuole — a large fluid-filled space containing cell sap (dissolved sugars and salts). It presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall, keeping the cell turgid and helping to support the plant structure.

Key Fact

Plant cells have three additional structures compared to animal cells: cell wall (cellulose, structural support), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and permanent vacuole (cell sap, turgidity). Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no true nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts.

Prokaryotic Cell Structure

Bacterial cells are prokaryotic: smaller, simpler and without membrane-bound organelles. Their genetic material is a single circular loop of DNA floating in the cytoplasm. Many bacteria also contain small, extra loops of DNA called plasmids, which can carry genes for antibiotic resistance and can be passed between bacteria. Bacteria do have ribosomes (for protein synthesis) and a cell wall (though made of a different material from plant cell walls, usually peptidoglycan).

From Hooke to the Electron Microscope

Light microscopes improved steadily after Hooke’s time. By the 19th century, biologists could see nuclei, cell divisions and the broad outlines of organelles. Light microscopes have a useful magnification of about ×1500 and a resolution of around 200 nm. To prepare a slide, a thin sample is placed on glass, stained (iodine to reveal plant cell walls and nuclei; methylene blue for animal cells), and covered with a coverslip lowered at an angle to avoid air bubbles.

The real breakthrough came in the 20th century with the invention of the electron microscope. Instead of light, it fires a beam of electrons at the specimen. This gives a resolution of around 0.2 nm — approximately 1,000 times better than a light microscope. Transmission electron microscopes (TEMs) can magnify specimens up to about two million times. This level of detail revealed the internal folds of mitochondria (cristae), the structure of ribosomes and the double membrane of the nucleus — all previously invisible. Each discovery confirmed and refined scientists’ models of cell structure.

The development of electron microscopy is a clear example of how scientific knowledge develops with technology (a key Ideas about Science theme): new instruments allow observations that lead to revised or extended explanations. Hooke proposed cells existed; electron microscopists revealed how they worked from the inside.

The magnification formula is: $$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}$$ Always convert both measurements to the same unit before dividing. Scientists often work in micrometres (µm) for cells and nanometres (nm) for organelles and molecules. \(1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ µm} = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ nm}\).

Worked example: A drawing of a cell measures 45 mm on the page. The actual cell is 0.015 mm. Magnification = \(\frac{45}{0.015} = \times 3000\). Always state the multiplication symbol and the number, e.g. ×3000. If asked to find the real size: real size = image size ÷ magnification.

Key Fact

Magnification = image size ÷ real size. Electron microscopes (~0.2 nm resolution, up to ×2,000,000) revealed mitochondrial cristae, ribosome structure and nuclear membrane detail that light microscopes (~200 nm resolution, ×1500) could not resolve.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Magnification calculations are reliably examined. The most common mistake is using different units for image size and real size — always convert to the same unit first. When asked to ‘explain’ how microscopy has improved our understanding of cells, the examiners want you to use causal language: state what the technology allowed scientists to see, then explain how this changed or extended the scientific explanation (model). Listing microscope types without linking them to specific discoveries will not score the highest marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eukaryotic cells (animals and plants) have a nucleus enclosing DNA; prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have a DNA loop in the cytoplasm and no true nucleus. Plant cells have three extra structures: cell wall, chloroplasts and permanent vacuole.
  • Organelle design matches function: mitochondrial cristae increase surface area for respiration; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis; the cell membrane’s receptor molecules enable chemical signalling.
  • Advances in microscopy — from Hooke’s light microscope to the electron microscope — progressively revealed finer detail. Magnification = image size ÷ real size. Electron microscopes offer around 1,000 times better resolution than light microscopes.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why electron microscopes rather than light microscopes were needed to discover the internal structure of mitochondria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mitochondrial internal structures (cristae, inner membrane folds) are measured in nanometres. The resolution of a light microscope is around 200 nm — insufficient to distinguish features this small. The electron microscope has a resolution of around 0.2 nm, around 1,000 times better, allowing structures of nanometre scale to be seen as separate objects. Without this resolution, the cristae would appear as a blurred mass within the mitochondrion.
Secure: Light microscope resolution too low; electron microscope resolution high enough to distinguish nanometre-scale features.
Developing: Electron microscopes magnify more.
Emerging: Electron microscopes are better.

practice_questions.text: The development of the electron microscope has been described as a major advance in scientific understanding of cells. Evaluate this claim, with reference to specific discoveries it enabled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Prior to electron microscopy, scientists could observe cells and nuclei with light microscopes but could not resolve internal organelle structure. The electron microscope (TEM) revealed the cristae of mitochondria — folded inner membranes that increase the surface area for respiration enzymes — explaining why mitochondria are efficient at ATP production. It also resolved ribosome structure and the double membrane of the nucleus. These discoveries confirmed and refined the cell theory model. However, electron microscopes cannot be used on living specimens (the preparation process kills cells), and the images require interpretation. So while the electron microscope enormously advanced structural biology, it has limitations for studying dynamic processes in living cells.
Secure: Two specific discoveries named and explained; evaluation includes at least one limitation.
Developing: One discovery and one limitation.
Emerging: General statement that electron microscopes show more detail.

lessons.title: Growth, Development and Stem Cells
lessons.description: How organisms grow, the role of cell division, and the science and ethics of stem-cell therapy.
lessons.content_html:
Growth Through Cell Division

A human being begins as a single fertilised cell no wider than a human hair. Over the following nine months, that cell divides billions of times, eventually producing the trillions of specialised cells that form a newborn baby. The key question in developmental biology is not just how cells divide, but how they become so different from one another — a liver cell, a neuron and a skin cell all contain identical DNA, yet they look and behave completely differently.

Mitosis is the form of cell division responsible for growth and repair in multicellular organisms. Before mitosis begins, during a phase called S phase, the cell’s DNA replicates so that every chromosome is copied. Then during mitosis itself, the copies are separated and two genetically identical daughter cells are produced, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. It is crucial to understand that DNA replication happens before mitosis starts, not during it.

Key Fact

DNA replication occurs during S phase, before mitosis begins — not during mitosis itself. Mitosis then separates the copied chromosomes to produce two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.

Cell Differentiation

Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised. Although every cell in the body contains the same DNA, different genes are switched on or off in different cell types. This means each specialised cell produces only the proteins needed for its specific function.

The design of specialised cells directly reflects their function. Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus — this removes the nucleus and increases the surface area for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin. Neurones have long axons that allow electrical impulses to travel over large distances quickly. Root hair cells have long thin extensions that dramatically increase their surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

Sperm cells have a streamlined head containing an acrosome (with enzymes to penetrate the egg), a midpiece packed with mitochondria to supply energy for swimming, and a long flagellum tail for motility. Every feature serves the single purpose of delivering genetic material to an egg.

Muscle cells (muscle fibres) are elongated cells that can shorten and extend. They contain large numbers of mitochondria (for ATP production during contraction) and specialised proteins (actin and myosin) that slide past each other to generate force. Cells with highly specific roles like these are the endpoint of the differentiation process.

Stem Cells: Undifferentiated and Versatile

Stem cells are cells that have not yet differentiated. They retain the ability to divide and produce cells that can become specialised. There are two main types of stem cell relevant to your course: embryonic stem cells and adult stem cells.

Embryonic stem cells are found in the embryo in the first few days after fertilisation. They are described as pluripotent — they can differentiate into any cell type in the body. This makes them potentially very useful for treating diseases caused by cell loss or damage, such as Parkinson’s disease, type 1 diabetes, or spinal cord injury.

Adult stem cells are found in specific tissues, such as bone marrow (which produces blood stem cells that can differentiate into all blood cell types). They are more limited than embryonic stem cells — they can only produce the range of cells relevant to their tissue. Bone marrow transplants, which replace diseased blood stem cells, are an established medical therapy using adult stem cells.

Scientists have developed a technique to take ordinary adult cells (such as skin cells) and “reprogramme” them genetically to behave like embryonic stem cells. These are called induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells). Because they can be made from a patient’s own cells, they would avoid the risk of immune rejection and sidestep many of the ethical concerns associated with embryonic stem cells. iPS cell research is an active and rapidly developing field.

Key Fact

Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can become any cell type. Adult stem cells (e.g. bone marrow) can only produce cells of their own tissue type. iPS cells are reprogrammed adult cells that regain pluripotency without using embryos.

The Ethics of Stem Cell Research

Using embryonic stem cells requires destroying a human embryo at an early stage of development (3–5 days old). This raises serious ethical questions. People who hold that human life begins at fertilisation argue that destroying any embryo is morally wrong, regardless of the medical benefits. Others argue that the potential to alleviate suffering for millions of people outweighs concerns about a cluster of cells at such an early stage, which has no consciousness or capacity for pain.

This is a genuine values-based disagreement, not a scientific one. The science can establish what embryonic stem cells are capable of and what risks they carry. But the question of whether they should be used involves moral, religious and philosophical judgements that science alone cannot resolve. Being able to separate these two types of question is itself an important scientific skill — the distinction between an evidence-based claim and a values-based claim.

Even setting ethics aside, stem cell therapy faces practical challenges. Transplanted cells may be rejected by the patient’s immune system, requiring immunosuppressant drugs that leave the patient vulnerable to infection. There is also a risk that undifferentiated stem cells could divide uncontrollably after transplantation, forming tumours. Researchers must demonstrate that transplanted cells differentiate correctly and integrate safely into the host tissue before therapies can be considered safe enough for widespread clinical use.

The risk–benefit framework applied here mirrors wider scientific decision-making: weighing evidence-based risks (immune rejection, tumour formation) against potential benefits (restored function for people with otherwise untreatable conditions) under conditions of uncertainty. This is a classic IaS4 scenario — science provides the risk data, but the decision about acceptable risk involves values as well as evidence.

Key Fact

The ethics of embryonic stem cell use involves values about when human life begins — a question science cannot answer. Practical risks include immune rejection and uncontrolled cell division (tumour risk). iPS cells and adult stem cells partially address both concerns.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions about stem cells and ethics, examiners want you to distinguish between scientific arguments (evidence about what stem cells can do, risks of rejection or tumour formation) and values-based arguments (beliefs about when human life begins, moral weight of potential cures). If you merge these, you lose marks. Always name the type of stem cell you are describing — ‘stem cell’ alone is insufficient. For the mitosis misconception: state clearly that DNA replication happens before mitosis, in S phase. Do not say DNA doubles ‘during mitosis’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells and is used for growth and repair. DNA replication occurs in S phase before mitosis begins. Differentiation produces specialised cells by switching genes on or off.
  • Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (any cell type). Adult stem cells are more limited. iPS cells are reprogrammed adult cells that regain pluripotency without using embryos.
  • Stem cell ethics involve both scientific evidence (risks, capabilities) and values (beliefs about embryonic life). Science can inform but cannot resolve the values-based dimension of the debate.

lessons.title: Transport, Circulation and Exchange Surfaces
lessons.description: Diffusion, osmosis, active transport, and why large organisms need lungs, intestines and a heart.
lessons.content_html:
Why Size Changes Everything

A single-celled organism like an amoeba gets all the oxygen it needs simply by diffusion across its cell surface. No circulatory system required. But a blue whale — the largest animal ever to have lived — needs a massive heart, kilometres of blood vessels, enormous lungs and elaborate exchange surfaces in its intestines. The fundamental reason is mathematics: as organisms grow, their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) decreases. The volume (and therefore the number of cells needing supplies) grows faster than the surface area available for exchange.

Consider cubes: a 1 cm cube has a surface area of 6 cm2 and a volume of 1 cm3 — SA:V ratio of 6:1. A 2 cm cube has a surface area of 24 cm2 and volume of 8 cm3 — SA:V ratio of only 3:1. A 3 cm cube has SA:V of 2:1. As the cube grows, its surface area–to–volume ratio halves and then halves again. For a large, complex organism, simple diffusion across the body surface cannot supply oxygen and nutrients fast enough to reach every cell.

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This means the surface area available for gas exchange and nutrient uptake is insufficient to supply all the cells by diffusion alone. Large organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

Moving Substances Across Cell Membranes

Cells exchange substances with their surroundings by three mechanisms. Diffusion is the passive net movement of particles down a concentration gradient — from high to low concentration. No energy is needed. Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out.

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion involving only water molecules moving through a partially permeable membrane. Water moves from a region of high water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of low water concentration (concentrated solution). This is important in, for example, kidney function and plant cell water regulation.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy in the form of ATP from respiration. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb nitrate ions from the soil even when their internal concentration already exceeds that in the soil. Intestinal epithelial cells also use active transport to absorb glucose from the gut lumen into the blood.

The rate of diffusion is increased by: a steeper concentration gradient (greater difference in concentration between the two sides); a larger surface area (more molecules can cross at once); a shorter diffusion distance (thinner membrane means less distance to travel); and a higher temperature (molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently).

These four factors explain the design of every specialised exchange surface in the body: alveoli have a huge surface area, very thin walls and are richly supplied with blood capillaries that maintain a steep gradient. Villi in the small intestine have a large surface area (with microvilli), a thin epithelium and a dense capillary network. Both surfaces are optimised to maximise diffusion rate.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy). Active transport requires ATP and moves substances against the concentration gradient. All three are essential for supplying cells — the correct mechanism depends on whether the substance moves with or against its gradient.

Specialised Exchange Surfaces

Because large organisms cannot rely on diffusion alone, evolution has produced highly specialised exchange surfaces shared by several structures in the body. All share the same design principles: large surface area, thin walls and a good supply of blood capillaries that maintain steep concentration gradients.

Alveoli are tiny air sacs clustered at the ends of the smallest airways (bronchioles). Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveolus, across the single-cell-thick alveolar wall and capillary wall, into the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction. The human lungs contain several hundred million alveoli, giving a combined surface area estimated at around 70 m2 in an average adult — roughly the floor area of a studio flat.

In lung diseases such as emphysema (caused primarily by smoking), alveolar walls break down, reducing the total surface area available for gas exchange. This means less oxygen enters the blood, leaving patients breathless even at rest. This clinical context illustrates why the design features of alveoli — surface area, thin wall, blood supply — are so important: any reduction in these factors directly reduces the efficiency of gas exchange.

Villi are finger-like projections that line the small intestine, increasing its surface area enormously. Each villus has a thin epithelium (one cell thick), a dense network of blood capillaries for absorbing glucose and amino acids into the blood, and a lacteal (lymph vessel) for absorbing fatty acids and glycerol. The epithelial cells themselves also have microvilli (tiny projections on their surface) that further multiply the surface area — this folded structure within a folded structure is a striking example of biological design maximising exchange.

The Circulatory System: Delivering and Collecting

Even with efficient exchange surfaces, substances still need to be transported throughout the body. In humans, this is achieved by the double circulatory system: one circuit carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs for gas exchange (the pulmonary circuit); a second carries oxygenated blood from the heart to all body tissues (the systemic circuit). Having two circuits maintains high blood pressure for efficient delivery.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand this. Veins carry blood back to the heart at lower pressure, with thinner walls and valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are the key exchange vessels: walls just one cell thick allow substances to diffuse efficiently between blood and surrounding tissues.

Key Fact

Capillaries, alveoli and villi all share the same design principle: thin walls (one cell thick), large total surface area and a good blood supply to maintain steep concentration gradients. These features maximise the rate of substance exchange.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For SA:V ratio questions, always show your working with the formula SA:V and include units (cm2:cm3). When asked to explain why alveoli or villi are efficient exchange surfaces, use all four design features: large surface area, thin wall (short diffusion distance), steep concentration gradient (maintained by blood supply), and moisture (for gas exchange). Missing one feature typically loses a mark. For ‘compare’ questions about diffusion and active transport, the key contrast is energy requirement and direction relative to the concentration gradient.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • As organisms grow, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This makes diffusion alone insufficient, requiring specialised exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi) and transport systems (the circulatory system).
  • Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy, down the gradient). Active transport uses ATP to move substances against the gradient. All three are essential in the body.
  • Efficient exchange surfaces share the same design: large surface area, thin walls (short diffusion distance), steep concentration gradient (maintained by blood flow). Capillaries, alveoli and villi all exemplify this design.

Supplemental oxygen increases the concentration of oxygen in inhaled air, steepening the gradient and partially compensating for reduced surface area, so more oxygen diffuses per breath despite the structural damage. A complete cure requires restoring alveolar structure, which is not currently possible.
Secure: Mechanism of damage linked to surface area reduction; gradient and diffusion rate explained; supplemental oxygen logic explained.

Emerging: Emphysema damages lungs; less oxygen absorbed.

lessons.title: Nervous System and Hormonal Coordination
lessons.description: Detecting stimuli, reflexes, and how hormones and nerves coordinate the body.
lessons.content_html:
The Nervous System

Your body constantly receives information from the world around you — light, temperature, sound, pain. The nervous system processes this information and produces fast, coordinated responses. It has two main divisions: the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system, the network of nerves connecting the CNS to every part of the body.

The pathway of a nervous response follows a fixed sequence: a stimulus is detected by a sensory receptor, which sends a signal along a sensory neurone to the CNS. A relay neurone within the CNS passes the signal to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector — a muscle that contracts or a gland that secretes. The result is a coordinated response.

Key Fact

The nervous pathway: stimulus → sensory receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The CNS processes information and coordinates the appropriate reaction.

Neurones and Synapses

There are three types of neurone. Sensory neurones carry signals from receptors to the CNS; relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; motor neurones carry signals from the CNS to effectors. All neurones have a cell body, dendrites (short branches that receive signals), and a long axon that transmits the electrical impulse. Many axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath, which speeds up signal transmission.

Where two neurones meet there is a tiny gap called a synapse. An electrical impulse cannot cross this gap directly. Instead, when the impulse reaches the end of the first neurone, chemical neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft. They diffuse across and bind to specific receptor molecules on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. Synapses ensure signals travel in one direction only and allow complex coordination across many pathways.

A reflex arc is a shorter version of the nervous pathway that produces automatic, protective responses. The signal travels through the spinal cord rather than all the way to the brain, which makes the response much faster. The pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector.

Consider touching a sharp object. Pain receptors in the skin detect the stimulus and send a signal along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord. A relay neurone immediately connects to a motor neurone, which stimulates the arm muscle to contract and pull the hand away — all before the brain has consciously registered pain. The brain receives the information afterwards, which is why you feel the sensation a fraction of a second after the withdrawal.

Reflexes are important because they have fewer synapses to cross and a shorter pathway, making them significantly faster than voluntary responses. Other reflexes include the pupil reflex (the pupil constricts in bright light to protect the retina) and the knee-jerk reflex.

Key Fact

Reflex arcs bypass the brain — the signal goes through the spinal cord only. This reduces the distance the signal must travel and the number of synapses to cross, making the response faster and protecting the body from harm before conscious awareness.

The Endocrine System

The endocrine system uses chemical messengers called hormones to coordinate and control body functions. Unlike the nervous system, which produces fast, short-lived, localised responses, the endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting and more widespread responses. Hormones travel in the blood to target organs; only cells with the correct receptor proteins will respond.

Key endocrine glands include the pituitary gland (the “master gland” that controls other glands), the thyroid gland (controls metabolic rate), the adrenal glands (produce adrenaline), and the pancreas (produces insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose). The ovaries and testes produce the sex hormones that control reproduction and secondary sexual characteristics.

Both systems coordinate the body, but they work in fundamentally different ways. The nervous system uses electrical impulses along neurones — responses are fast (fractions of a second), short-lived and precise (a specific muscle contracts). The endocrine system uses hormones in the blood — responses are slower (seconds to hours), longer-lasting and widespread (affecting many tissues at once).

A useful way to remember this: nervous = fast, precise, short (like a phone call); endocrine = slow, widespread, sustained (like a broadcast message). Many physiological processes are coordinated by both systems working together — for example, the “fight or flight” response involves both nerve impulses and the release of adrenaline from the adrenal glands.

The ruler drop test is a classic investigation of reaction time. One person holds a ruler vertically while their partner places thumb and finger at the 0 cm mark. When the ruler is released without warning, the partner catches it as quickly as possible. A shorter distance fallen means a faster reaction time.

To design a reliable investigation, you must consider: what variable you are testing (e.g. does caffeine improve reaction time?), what you will keep constant (same ruler, same person catching, same hand position), how to reduce random error (repeat at least five times and calculate a mean, discard anomalous results). When writing a hypothesis, you should provide a scientific justification — for example, “caffeine is predicted to decrease reaction time because it is a stimulant that increases neurotransmitter activity at synapses.” A prediction states the expected outcome for a specific measurement, while a hypothesis explains why you expect it. These are not the same thing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to ‘explain’ how a reflex arc works, always state that the signal travels through the spinal cord, not the brain, and explain why this makes it faster (shorter pathway, fewer synapses). Use causal language: ‘because’, ‘so that’, ‘this means’. For compare questions on the nervous and endocrine systems, give a feature for each side (e.g. speed, duration, messenger type) rather than describing just one system.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nervous system carries electrical signals along neurones; the pathway stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector produces coordinated responses.
  • Reflex arcs bypass the brain, routing signals through the spinal cord only — this makes reflexes faster and protects the body from danger before conscious awareness.
  • The endocrine system uses hormones in the blood; responses are slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses but affect a wider range of tissues simultaneously.

lessons.title: Homeostasis: Glucose, Water and Temperature
lessons.description: Negative feedback, blood glucose control, diabetes, kidney function and thermoregulation.
lessons.content_html:
What is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is how your body keeps its internal conditions within narrow, safe limits. Enzymes and metabolic reactions function best at specific temperatures, pH levels and ion concentrations — drift too far from these ideal conditions and cells stop working efficiently, or stop working altogether. Every homeostatic system has three components working together: receptors detect a change; a coordination centre (such as the brain or pancreas) processes the information; effectors (muscles or glands) produce the corrective response.

All these systems use the same underlying control mechanism: negative feedback. When a condition rises above its set point, the body acts to bring it down. When it falls below, the body acts to bring it up. Once the set point is restored, the response switches off. This self-correcting loop keeps internal conditions stable despite constant change.

Key Fact

Homeostasis uses negative feedback: receptor detects change → coordination centre processes signal → effector produces corrective response → condition returns to normal → response switches off. This applies to blood glucose, water balance and temperature.

Controlling Blood Glucose

Blood glucose concentration rises after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal and falls during exercise or between meals. The pancreas acts as both the receptor and coordination centre. When blood glucose rises, the pancreas secretes insulin. Insulin causes body cells — especially muscle and liver cells — to take up glucose from the blood. The liver converts the excess into glycogen for storage. These actions bring blood glucose back down to its normal range.

When blood glucose falls, the pancreas secretes glucagon. Glucagon signals the liver to break stored glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood. Insulin and glucagon work in opposite directions — this opposing action is how negative feedback achieves precise control.

In a glucose tolerance test, a person drinks a standard glucose solution. Their blood glucose level is measured at regular intervals for two hours. A typical result for a person without diabetes: blood glucose rises steeply in the first 30–60 minutes as the glucose is absorbed, then returns to near-normal within two hours as insulin triggers glucose uptake.

For someone with Type 1 diabetes, the trace looks different: blood glucose rises to a much higher level and stays elevated, because the pancreas produces little or no insulin. For Type 2 diabetes, blood glucose also stays elevated but may rise more slowly because some insulin is still produced. Identifying these differences from a graph is a common examination task. When describing a correlation in data like this, remember that correlation does not prove causation — the elevated blood glucose is caused by insulin deficiency, not simply “caused by” the glucose drink itself.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Without insulin, blood glucose cannot be lowered after eating, so it rises to dangerously high levels. Treatment requires regular insulin injections or an insulin pump, alongside careful monitoring of blood glucose and carbohydrate intake. Type 1 usually develops in childhood or early adulthood and cannot be prevented.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when body cells become resistant to insulin — they do not respond properly even when insulin is present. The pancreas may produce some insulin but its effect is reduced. Blood glucose stays elevated because cells do not absorb it efficiently. Type 2 is strongly linked to obesity and a sedentary lifestyle, and is becoming more common worldwide. Treatment focuses on dietary changes (reducing sugar intake), regular exercise and, when needed, medication. In some cases insulin injections may eventually be required.

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: pancreas does not produce insulin (autoimmune) — treated with insulin injections. Type 2 diabetes: body cells become resistant to insulin (often linked to obesity) — treated with diet, exercise and medication. Mixing these up is one of the most common errors in biology exams.

Water Balance and the Kidneys

The kidneys filter the blood and control the concentration of water, ions and urea in the body — a process called osmoregulation. Excess water, ions and the waste product urea are removed as urine. The hormone ADH (anti-diuretic hormone), produced by the pituitary gland, controls how much water the kidneys reabsorb. When you are dehydrated, more ADH is released, the kidneys reabsorb more water, and urine becomes concentrated. When you are well hydrated, less ADH is released, and urine is more dilute.

Temperature Regulation

Human body temperature is maintained at approximately 37°C by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain. It receives signals from temperature receptors in the skin (monitoring external temperature) and in the blood (monitoring core temperature). When body temperature rises too high, cooling responses are triggered: vasodilation increases blood flow to the skin surface so heat is lost by radiation; sweat glands produce sweat that evaporates from the skin, transferring heat energy away from the body.

When body temperature falls too low, warming responses are triggered: vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, conserving heat; muscles shiver (rapid involuntary contractions that generate heat from respiration); body hairs stand up, trapping an insulating layer of air close to the skin.

If thermoregulation fails, the consequences can be life-threatening. Hypothermia occurs when core body temperature drops well below 37°C — cellular enzymes begin to function too slowly, reflexes slow, and in severe cases organs can fail. Heat stroke occurs when the body overheats beyond its cooling capacity — sweating may cease, enzymes begin to denature, and organ damage can result. Both conditions illustrate why maintaining a stable internal temperature is so critical for enzyme function and metabolism.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For any homeostasis question, structure your answer using the three-component framework: receptor (what detects the change), coordination centre (what processes it), effector (what corrects it). For extended-response questions, make sure you explain the negative feedback loop — not just what happens, but why the response switches off once the set point is restored. When interpreting blood glucose graphs, state the direction and extent of the change and link it to the relevant hormone before drawing a conclusion about the condition shown.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis maintains stable internal conditions using negative feedback: a change is detected, a corrective response is triggered, and the response switches off once the set point is restored.
  • Blood glucose is controlled by insulin (lowers glucose, triggers storage as glycogen) and glucagon (raises glucose, triggers release from glycogen). Failure of this system causes diabetes — Type 1 (no insulin) or Type 2 (insulin resistance).
  • Temperature regulation uses vasodilation and sweating to cool, and vasoconstriction and shivering to warm — all coordinated by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain.

lessons.title: Reproduction, Hormones and Failing Organs
lessons.description: The menstrual cycle, contraception, IVF, and how organ failure is treated.
lessons.content_html:
The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle prepares the female body for potential pregnancy each month. It is controlled by four interacting hormones that form a complex feedback system. Understanding the timing and role of each hormone is essential for explaining contraception and fertility treatment.

The four hormones and their roles: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the maturation of an egg inside a follicle in the ovary. As the follicle matures, it produces oestrogen. Oestrogen has three effects: it causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair after menstruation, it inhibits further FSH production (negative feedback), and it stimulates a surge of LH. The LH surge (around day 14 of the cycle) triggers ovulation — the release of the mature egg from the ovary. After ovulation, the empty follicle (now called the corpus luteum) produces progesterone, which maintains the thickened uterus lining ready for implantation. If fertilisation does not occur, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins, restarting the cycle.

Key Fact

FSH stimulates egg maturation → oestrogen thickens uterus lining and triggers LH surge → LH causes ovulation → progesterone maintains lining. If no pregnancy, progesterone drops → menstruation begins.

Hormonal methods of contraception include the combined pill (containing synthetic oestrogen and progesterone), the progesterone-only mini-pill, implants and injections. These work by maintaining artificially high levels of these hormones, which inhibit FSH production from the pituitary gland. Without FSH, no egg matures, so ovulation does not occur. Hormonal methods are highly effective but can have side effects including headaches and, rarely, increased risk of blood clots.

Non-hormonal methods include condoms (a barrier method that prevents sperm reaching the egg and also protects against sexually transmitted infections), diaphragms (placed over the cervix), copper IUDs (create an environment hostile to sperm), and surgical sterilisation (permanent). When evaluating contraceptive methods, consider effectiveness, reversibility, protection against infections, side effects and convenience — the right choice depends on individual circumstances.

Some people have difficulty conceiving naturally. Fertility treatments use hormones to assist. FSH injections can stimulate ovulation in women whose pituitary gland does not produce sufficient FSH naturally — this is called ovulation induction.

In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a more complex treatment. FSH is used to stimulate the ovaries to produce several eggs at once. These are collected surgically and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory dish. The embryos are allowed to develop for a few days before one or two are transferred into the uterus. IVF raises important questions about balancing benefits (allowing parenthood for those who cannot conceive naturally) against risks (physical and emotional demands on the patient, the fate of unused embryos) and costs. This kind of risk–benefit reasoning under uncertainty is at the heart of how science informs medical decisions.

When Organs and Control Systems Fail

When key organs fail, medical technology can take over their function — but there are always trade-offs between different treatments. The kidney is a good example. Healthy kidneys filter the blood and remove waste products (especially urea), maintain ion balance and regulate water content. When kidneys fail, waste products accumulate to life-threatening levels.

Two main approaches exist for treating kidney failure. Dialysis uses a machine to filter the blood artificially. Blood flows from the patient through a membrane into a dialysate solution; waste products (urea, excess ions) move across the membrane by diffusion into the solution, while needed substances remain in the blood. Dialysis must be done regularly — typically several sessions a week, each lasting several hours. This places a significant burden on the patient’s time and quality of life, but it does not require surgery and can be maintained long-term.

Kidney transplant involves receiving a healthy kidney from a donor (either a living donor or a recently deceased donor). A successful transplant restores full kidney function and frees the patient from dialysis. However, the patient must take immunosuppressant drugs for life to prevent the immune system from rejecting the donated organ. These drugs increase the risk of infections and other complications. Donors and recipients must be carefully matched to reduce rejection risk, and there are far fewer kidneys available than patients who need them.

Key Fact

Dialysis filters blood artificially — regular sessions required, no surgery, sustainable long-term. Kidney transplant restores full function but requires lifelong immunosuppressants and depends on donor availability. The decision between them involves weighing clinical, personal and logistical factors.

The kidney is not the only organ that can fail. Heart failure can be managed with medication, mechanical assist devices, or — in severe cases — a heart transplant. Liver failure may require a liver transplant (the liver can partially regenerate, so living donors can donate a segment). Pancreatic beta cell failure (Type 1 diabetes) is managed with insulin replacement rather than organ transplant, though research into islet cell transplantation is ongoing. In every case, the principles are the same: understand what function has been lost, weigh the available interventions, and consider both the benefits and the risks for the individual patient.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about the menstrual cycle, always link each hormone to its source gland and its specific effect — don’t just name the hormone. For IVF or organ failure questions, the command word ‘evaluate’ means you must discuss benefits and risks, then reach a supported conclusion. Avoid one-sided answers. Use precise causal language: ‘oestrogen inhibits FSH production, which prevents further egg maturation’ scores better than ‘oestrogen stops FSH.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in a feedback loop. FSH matures the egg; oestrogen thickens the lining and triggers the LH surge; LH causes ovulation; progesterone maintains the lining.
  • Hormonal contraception inhibits FSH, preventing ovulation. IVF uses FSH to stimulate multiple egg production and raises ethical questions about benefits, risks and the fate of unused embryos.
  • When organs fail, treatments aim to replace lost function. Kidney failure can be managed with dialysis (regular, no surgery) or transplant (full function restored but requires immunosuppressants and donor availability).

lessons.title: Evolution, Classification and Biodiversity
lessons.description: Natural selection, speciation, classification and protecting threatened biodiversity.
lessons.content_html:
How Was the Theory of Evolution Developed? (IaS3)

Scientific theories do not appear fully formed — they are built gradually from observations, hypotheses and accumulating evidence. The theory of evolution by natural selection is a powerful example of this process. Charles Darwin (1809–1882) developed his ideas during a five-year voyage around the world, recording variation in animals and plants across different environments. His observations of finch beak shapes on the Galápagos Islands — each suited to a different food source — helped him form the idea that species change in response to their environment over many generations.

Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) reached similar conclusions independently during fieldwork in South America and Southeast Asia. He and Darwin jointly presented their ideas to the Linnean Society in 1858. Their combined evidence — from different continents and different organisms — strengthened the case that natural selection was a real and general process, not just an observation specific to one place. This is an important example of how scientific explanations develop: independent evidence from multiple sources makes a theory more robust.

Key Fact

Natural selection works in four steps: (1) variation exists within a population; (2) individuals compete for limited resources; (3) those with the most advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive and reproduce; (4) advantageous alleles are inherited by the next generation. Over many generations, this changes the characteristics of the population.

Evidence for Evolution

Multiple independent lines of evidence support the theory of evolution. The fossil record shows gradual changes in the structure of organisms over geological time — transitional fossils show intermediate forms between ancestral and modern species. Comparative anatomy reveals similar bone structures across very different animals (such as the human arm, bat wing and whale flipper), suggesting they share common ancestors. DNA analysis shows that closely related species share more DNA sequences than distantly related ones — a finding that was entirely unknown to Darwin and Wallace, yet confirms their theory from a completely independent direction.

The peppered moth provides a well-documented example of natural selection observed over a short timescale. Before industrialisation, pale-coloured moths were camouflaged against lichen-covered trees and survived in greater numbers; dark (melanic) moths were more visible to predators and were rarer. When industrial pollution killed the lichens and darkened tree bark with soot, dark moths gained a survival advantage and became more common. After the introduction of pollution controls, pale moths became dominant again. This demonstrates that the direction of natural selection depends on the environment — and can reverse when conditions change.

Speciation occurs when a population becomes geographically or reproductively isolated. Once isolated, each group is exposed to different environmental pressures and accumulates different mutations through random genetic change. Over many generations, the two groups diverge until they are so genetically different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring — at this point they are considered separate species. Extinction occurs when a species cannot adapt quickly enough; the fossil record documents this throughout Earth's history.

It is important to remember that individuals do not evolve — populations evolve over many generations as the frequency of advantageous alleles increases. Evolution has no direction or goal; it simply reflects which traits happen to be best suited to the current environment.

Classification and Phylogenetic Trees

Classification is the process of grouping organisms based on their evolutionary relationships. The traditional Linnaean hierarchy (kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species) has been refined with modern DNA evidence. Phylogenetic trees show how species are related by shared ancestry — the more recently two species share a common ancestor, the more similar their DNA.

Modern classification uses evolutionary (phylogenetic) classification rather than grouping organisms solely by appearance. Two organisms can look similar because they share a recent common ancestor (homology) or because they evolved similar features independently in response to similar environments (convergent evolution). DNA evidence helps distinguish between these possibilities.

Darwin’s original theory was based on observed variation and the fossil record. Wallace’s independent observations from a different continent added further support. Since then, genetics, molecular biology and direct observation of evolution in bacteria and insects have added independent lines of evidence. When a theory is supported by multiple, independent strands of evidence from different disciplines, it becomes extremely well established. This is why evolution is one of the most strongly supported theories in all of science, despite being controversial when first proposed.

A key skill in science is recognising the difference between data (what is measured) and explanation (why it happens). The fossil record is data; natural selection is the explanation for why it shows the patterns it does. Both are needed for a complete scientific account.

Biodiversity and Its Threats

Biodiversity — the variety of species and genetic diversity within species — is essential for healthy ecosystems. Greater biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change; loss of species can cause cascading effects through food webs. Human activities are the primary cause of the current rapid decline in biodiversity worldwide: habitat destruction (especially deforestation), pollution, overexploitation of species, introduction of invasive species, and climate change all reduce biodiversity at rates far exceeding natural background extinction levels.

Key Fact

Biodiversity is threatened by habitat destruction, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change. These all reduce biodiversity at rates much faster than natural processes, destabilising ecosystems and reducing their resilience.

Conservation strategies aim to protect biodiversity and allow natural ecosystems to recover. Protected areas (national parks, nature reserves) limit damaging human activity in key habitats. Captive breeding programmes maintain viable populations of endangered species in zoos, with the aim of eventual reintroduction to the wild. Seed banks preserve the genetic diversity of plant species as insurance against extinction. Fishing quotas and logging regulations prevent over-exploitation of natural resources. Reforestation projects restore destroyed habitats and increase carbon absorption.

Effective conservation requires long-term scientific monitoring to assess whether biodiversity is recovering, and international cooperation since many threatened species and habitats cross national borders. Scientific data from monitoring programmes informs policy decisions — but these decisions also involve economic trade-offs and values, not just science.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For evolution questions, always apply the four-step mechanism (variation → competition → survival of the fittest → inheritance of advantageous alleles) to the specific organism and environment in the question. Don’t give a generic definition — apply the science to the context. For IaS3-style questions about how evidence builds a scientific explanation, identify multiple independent sources of evidence and explain why multiple independent lines of evidence are more convincing than a single source. When asked about biodiversity threats, name the specific human activity and explain the mechanism by which it reduces species diversity.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Evolution by natural selection was proposed independently by Darwin and Wallace from observations in different parts of the world. The theory is now supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: fossils, comparative anatomy and DNA.
  • Speciation occurs when isolated populations diverge through different selection pressures until they can no longer interbreed. Classification now uses DNA-based phylogenetic trees to reflect true evolutionary relationships.
  • Biodiversity is threatened by human activities including habitat destruction, pollution and overexploitation. Conservation strategies include protected areas, breeding programmes, seed banks and reforestation.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their advantageous alleles to the next generation.
The formation of a new species when populations of the same species become isolated and evolve independently until they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Branching diagrams that represent the evolutionary relationships between groups of organisms based on shared characteristics and DNA evidence.
Classification based on evolutionary relationships using DNA evidence, also called cladistics.
The variety of living organisms in a given area, including the number of different species and the genetic variation within species.
The permanent disappearance of a species when no living individuals remain, often caused by inability to adapt to environmental change, new predators or habitat destruction.
Differences in the characteristics of individuals of the same species, arising from genetic differences, environmental differences, or both.
